strengths: Tackles a genuinely novel and severely ill-posed problem: reconstructing full hyperspectral images from a single filterless panchromatic snapshot with only chromatic-aberration cues, going beyond prior filter-array or multi-optic systems.

The core technical contribution—patch-based conditional diffusion with cross-patch PSF-consistency guidance during sampling—is well-motivated and cleanly formulated (scale ambiguity resolution via least-squares closed-form patch rescaling, gradient-based consistency guidance), and is shown to be essential via convincing ablations (Table 2, Fig. 6a) rather than just increased model capacity (UNet-Regress baseline).

Strong and extensive empirical validation: simulation benchmarks against 8 SOTA baselines with clear margins (2.86 dB PSNR gain), cross-dataset generalization to ICVL/Harvard/CAVE without finetuning, a real fabricated metalens prototype with full calibration pipeline, and even a demonstration of applicability to an unrelated system (CASSI) showing the guidance framework generalizes beyond the primary filterless setting.

The per-pixel uncertainty quantification from multiple diffusion samples is a valuable byproduct, empirically validated with strong Pearson correlations to true error in both simulation (0.80) and real experiments (0.69), and shown useful for selecting/pruning unreliable pixels (CASSI truncation experiment).

Thorough and honest supplementary material covering PSF designs, fabrication, calibration, noise robustness, interpretability (saliency maps matching PSF structure), and failure-mode analysis (homogeneous regions), which strengthens reproducibility and scientific rigor.
Physically grounded and interpretable analysis of PSF/lens design trade-offs (Table 3, Fig. 6b) linking optical design choices to reconstruction quality and model behavior.
weaknesses: Baselines are not originally designed for the filterless, large-PSF-support setting; while the authors acknowledge this and add a Bayer-filtered comparison, the primary comparison in Table 1 could be seen as somewhat unfair to methods architected for different (better-conditioned) forward models, slightly limiting how conclusive the head-to-head numbers are.

Reconstruction is computationally expensive (up to 52 minutes/scene for higher-resolution datasets), which the authors note limits applicability to real-time settings; mitigations are proposed but not fully evaluated in the main results.

The method inherently fails on spatially homogeneous regions (acknowledged limitation), and because patches are optimized independently with only boundary-level coupling via guidance, global scene context/semantics cannot propagate, leading to uneven quality within a scene (e.g., large uniform flower regions in Fig. 5).

The experimental prototype relies on a small, imperfectly registered finetuning dataset (6 tabletop scenes with only homography-based alignment and simulated jitter augmentation to compensate for misalignment), which, while reasonably justified, still leaves some uncertainty about how much of the good real-world performance is attributable to this particular calibration/finetuning recipe versus general applicability of the approach.

Real-scene evaluation uses a modest number of test scenes (8), with performance varying substantially across scenes (PSNR 27.5–35.0 dB), and objects are relatively simple/controlled tabletop items rather than natural in-the-wild scenes, so broader external validity is not yet demonstrated.
